lines.text: Hi, I'm Sindy! In this last episode, your AI assistant takes the wheel.
Your AI assistant already writes your code. Why not let it build the Slurm cluster too, and help you debug it?
Picture this: you work in your editor, with Claude, Copilot or Cursor in the side panel.
You'd like it to create a cluster, check its status and manage its nodes, while you keep coding.
All you need is sind, Docker, and an assistant that speaks MCP.
First, a quick refresher. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, connects an AI assistant to servers that offer tools.
The assistant is the client. A server describes its tools: their names, what they do, and the arguments they take.
When your request needs a tool, the assistant calls it. You can approve the call first, and the result flows back.
Client and server talk over standard input and output, or over HTTP, and sind speaks both.
Let's connect sind. Run sind mcp claude enable, and Claude Desktop knows about it.
VS Code and Cursor work the same way, with their own names. Disable undoes it.
Prefer to edit the config yourself? This entry makes your editor run sind mcp start, which serves the tools over standard input and output.
To see every tool, sind mcp tools writes their definitions to a JSON file.
Each sind command becomes a tool, named after it with underscores, like sind create cluster or sind get nodes.
Every tool also wears a label: read-only for the get tools, destructive for create, delete, exec and most power tools.
Your client uses these hints to decide when to ask you first.
A few commands stay out: enter and ssh, which need a terminal, the two that print secrets, and the ones that only print help.
Now, let's drive! You ask for a cluster, and a look at its nodes.
The assistant picks sind create cluster. It's marked destructive, so read its flags before you approve.
Then it calls sind get nodes, which is read-only and always answers in JSON.
Every call hands back the command's output, its errors, and its exit code.
Later, your jobs aren't starting. You ask what's wrong.
The assistant can look around with read-only tools: sind get cluster for health, sind logs, and sind doctor.
And if it wants to reboot a node, sind power reboot is destructive, so your client can check with you first.
About that exit code: sind exec passes on the status of the command it ran, here forty-two.
The sind exec tool returns that status as its exit code. A call whose arguments sind rejects reads two: change the call, don't retry it.
To serve several clients at once, run sind mcp stream. It speaks HTTP, here on port eighty eighty.
Its output tells you where the bearer token lives, without showing it, plus a client config to paste.
The loopback address keeps other hosts out, and the token keeps out other users of your machine.
Be careful, though: the tools are not sandboxed. They run sind with all of your Docker access.
Check the flags of every create call before approving, and use data volume to keep your host files out of the cluster.
The rule of thumb: if you wouldn't let an agent run sind for you, don't give it these tools.
To recap: a single command hooks up your assistant, each sind command turns into a tool, and you stay in charge of what changes.
You made it through the whole course! Next up: pick a guide that fits your work. Happy clustering!
